speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Strong families are, and must remain, the basic building blocks of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: For each of our families and our society, children are our future.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: With strong families and good support from society, our children can have a good start in life.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: In the coming years, my Ministry will continue to strengthen fundamental family relationships and support vulnerable families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Fathers play an important role in parenting, and shared parental responsibility should become a way of life in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Employers who agree to grant this extra week of leave to employees may seek reimbursement from the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This is on top of the one week of paternity leave we have today, which is compulsory and which the Government pays for.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This additional week should allow fathers to be more active in raising their children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Public Service took the lead by implementing this immediately.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Since the NDR announcement on 23 August 2015, enlightened employers have been granting their employees the extra week of paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This Bill allows employers to seek reimbursement for the leave taken by eligible employees.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Eligible self-employed persons can likewise claim the loss of income from the Government for the additional week of leave taken.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The reimbursement can take place from 1 July 2016, when the system is ready.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Employers will still be reimbursed for leave taken from 24 August 2015 to 30 June 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This will be done in the next round of amendments to the Child Development Co-savings Act (CDCA), together with the enhancements to the other leave schemes announced at NPTD's COS.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Children of unwed parents may be disadvantaged and require more support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Child Development Co-Savings Scheme encourages unwed parents to contribute to the child's CDA for his or her development needs, and the amount will be matched by the Government up to a cap.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As CDA funds can only be used for approved educational and healthcare-related uses for the child, this can help to enhance the child's outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We are doing up the system enhancement concurrently for this to kick in, likely for children born from the third quarter of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The longer paid leave will provide unwed mothers with more time to care for their child in the early months.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This provision will be included in the next round of CDCA amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and the National Council of Social Services (NCSS) will also work with the relevant VWOs and agencies to strengthen support for families with vulnerable, low-income unwed mothers.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This is to enable them to make better-informed decisions to improve their financial and family stability and, ultimately, enhance their child's outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I do seek Parliament's agreement for the amendments, so that we can support families where it matters most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2012, in the Chinese zodiac Year of the Dragon, citizen births increased to over 33,000 babies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The good news is that citizen births in the last two years have matched the auspicious Year of the Dragon.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is some hope that we have turned the corner with regard to falling birth rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is still too early to tell whether the increased birth rate is a trend or a temporary rise due to positive sentiments brought about by the SG50 Jubilee celebrations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will touch on the optimistic part first.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am optimistic because I believe the Government has been addressing the structural obstacles to higher birth rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2013, the Workers' Party (WP), in response to the Government's Population White Paper, published its own population policy paper after the White Paper debate in this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In WP's paper, we elaborated on seven obstacles that stood in the way of higher birth rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, lack of work-life balance; two, escalating housing costs; three, income inequality; four, stressful education system; five, gender inequality in the family with regard to housework and childcare; six, pro-birth policies favouring higher income families; and seven, discrimination towards single-parent families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has been addressing some of these issues in the last few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this Bill, the Government is further enhancing paternity leave and is also addressing the last two structural obstacles that we have brought up: discrimination towards single-parent families and pro-birth policies favouring higher-income families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have been arguing that, while having children inside of marriage should continue to be encouraged, the children born to unwed parents should not be denied the benefits that children of married parents received.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe no children deserve to be disadvantaged and psychologically damaged for the norms their parents break.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 2(b) of this Bill expands the eligibility of the CDA co-savings scheme to "any other child", without amending the purpose of the Act, which is to, "encourage married women to have more children".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This amendment achieves the dual goals of encouraging births within marriage without discriminating against the children of unwed parents that we have called for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have also argued that the CDA scheme privileges higher-income families with the spare cash to put away into CDA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, as the quantum increases from $6,000 for each of the first two children, to $12,000 each for the third and fourth child, and $18,000 each for the fifth child and beyond, this actually encourages higher-income couples who could make the larger savings to have more children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It does so by establishing baseline savings for all children, regardless of the household income background.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a good first step by the Government in addressing the inequalities facing families seeking to have children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there are reasons to be optimistic because of the Government's policy reversals and advancement, we should be very cautious in our optimism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have the benefit of hindsight in the struggle against low birth rates for nearly 30 years now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's TFR fell below the replacement level of 2.1 in 1976 and reached the first low of 1.4 in 1986.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 1987, the Government's policy reversal from promoting birth control to encouraging Singaporeans to have more children, helped push the birth rate up in the following years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of the young couples having children today were born during the mini-baby boom caused by the policy reversal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the TFR resumed its gradual decline in the 1990s to hit the low of 1.4 in 2001 again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In reaction to the plunging TFR, the Government then launched the Baby Bonus scheme, which slowed the decline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the decline continued through the 2000s till TFR reached the lowest in 2010.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, the Government's pro-birth policy is important and can be effective in halting or slowing down birth rate declines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, most of the pro-birth policy changes have been reactive rather than proactive with the 1987 reversal reacting to the low in 1986, the Baby Bonus scheme reacting to the low in 2001, and the enhancements in the last few years reacting to the lowest in 2010.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This reactiveness limits the effectiveness of pro-birth policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of reacting to plunges and new lows in birth rates, I believe the Government should set a target of achieving a TFR of 1.4 in 2020 and a TFR of 1.7 by 2030.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will change the tone of the issue from being marked as a demographic problem to be struggled with to a performance target to be achieved, on par with many of the Government's socio-economic policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, the TFR is as much a socioeconomic issue as it is a demographic one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other lesson to be had here is that policies need to go beyond the carrot-and-stick approach and take a whole-of-Government approach to be effective over the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this respect, there is one dot that the Government has not connected to the birth rate issue, and it should.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One reason why pro-birth policies seem to be swimming against the tide in the 1990s and 2000s was because Singaporeans experienced growing socio-economic inequality and lingering gender inequality in those two decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has been shown in many studies in other developed countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On this issue, I would like to make three points.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As more fathers take on more responsibility in childcare, pro-birth policies, such as those promoting flexi-work arrangements should adapt to help fathers realise their parenting aspirations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As employer and management mind-sets start to change due to the Government's promotion of flexi-work arrangements through the Work-Life Grant, it would be important to help mould the new mind-sets to emphasise that flexi-work arrangements are not meant only or mainly for working mothers but should be made as accessible to working fathers too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this respect, the Government will need to change its own mindset that establishes a hard association between mothers and childcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should also consider rewording section 3, subsection 1(a) of the Act which I quoted earlier, to, "encourage married couples to have more children", instead of "married women".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is so as to emphasise in our laws that the state does not place the burden of birth rates and thus the blame of low births solely on the motivations of women but recognise that the decision to have children and the raising of children are the shared responsibility of both spouses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The wording of the CDCA should be thoroughly looked at to emphasise this shared responsibility to have and raise more children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, since the Act has expanded beyond the original monetary co-savings carrot, the Government should also consider renaming the Act to reflect the contents more accurately and better, symbolically, perhaps as the Family Life Promotion Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, we should extend the equality of benefits to all men and women who are parents of Singaporean children as far as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This includes single unwed parents and also the non-citizen spouses of Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may not seem related to the birth rates of married citizen couples at first glance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we are all social beings living in communities of shared interests in the first instance, not detached individuals with selfish interests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we have seen in this House, Members from across the political spectrum have strongly empathised with single unwed mothers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is something universal in this sentiment, as those of us who have or aspire to have children cannot bear to see other children suffer through no fault of their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Extending equality to all parents of Singaporean children cultivates positive sentiments for having babies and raising children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also a good time to look at the housing needs of children of single unwed parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As it is, this group of single parents is prevented from buying a new or resale Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat until they are 35 years old to go under the Single Singapore Citizen Scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This creates an unacceptable inequality where Permanent Residents benefit more from HDB home ownership than a group of citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More importantly, the children are denied a stable physical and social environment to grow up in to focus on their schooling and playing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The empathy for suffering Singaporean children and their parents also extends to non-citizen spouses who struggle with residential security due to the need to constantly renew visit passes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are economically rational and both short-term and long-term financial security affect their decisions to have more babies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CDA First Step grant is a welcome move towards narrowing the gap in child development resources between low-income and high-income households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is then up to the parents to match the grant by topping up the CDA up to another $10,000 to earn higher interest and earmark savings for the child's education and well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government could create incentives for parents to make the additional savings by making the savings eligible for income tax reliefs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason we are calling for a standardised grant for each child instead of the stepwise $6,000, $12,000 and $18,000 formula for the CDA grants is because short-term financial security is a factor, especially for lower-income and middle-income households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The stepwise formula is meant to be carrots to entice parents to have three babies or more but ignores the fact that the immediate stress and cost of raising existing children would put off parents from deciding on the third baby.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am cautiously optimistic that the Government has finally found the verve after three decades to stop blaming Singaporeans for not choosing to have babies and to start addressing the structural obstacles to enable Singaporeans to have more babies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also stand in full support of this Bill because it is not only about  dollars and cents but also about the hours, the minutes and the seconds, the precious time we spend with our children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments to section 3 bring about a stronger sense of inclusiveness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Single unwed mothers do not enjoy most of the benefits and support given to married mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You do not have to be a single parent to realise the difficulties they go through and  face in bringing up their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: No matter what the circumstances are that led to them being single unwed mothers, we should still help and support them, especially their child or children who, like us, are fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I mentioned during the Committee of Supply (COS) debates, to be a truly inclusive society, we need to accord equal rights to our single unwed mothers, and we should ensure that they do not feel alone in their journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Together with MSF, we have fought hard for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have joined 16 other Members of Parliament (MPs), Non-Constituency MPs (NCMPs) and Nominated MPs (NMPs) and the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) who, over the 12 years, spoke up for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The change in this policy is timely and I do hope that this does open the floodgates of help and support for single unwed mothers and the days of penalising them are history and they will finally get the same high level of support we give to our married mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this Bill does not just talk about mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also emphasises the important role fathers play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Research at the University of Bergen has shown that, and I quote, "A sensitive and attentive father has a positive influence on a child's development, but only if he spends a considerable amount of time with his child during his first year".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This research is part of a major project at The Norwegian Centre for Child Behavioural Development.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I urge the Government to do more, to not just do more in providing financial grants, which is important, but also do more in helping to ensure that both fathers and mothers have the chance to spend more time with their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government is now writing this next and brand-new chapter in this journey, and we now need employers and fathers to join us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Tan had previously stated that in 2013, only 28% of fathers took up the Government-paid Paternity Leave; in 2014, the figure was 36%.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I sincerely hope that employers will not only grant the fathers their paternity leave but also actively encourage them to take it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My appeal for fathers, speaking up as a father, is that you will not regret spending time, quality time, with your children in this amazing journey called parenthood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a journey that changes your life, that makes you a better person, and this is a journey your children need you to play an active role in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have gone from being the biggest Linkin Park fan to now being the biggest Pororo Park fan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And quite embarrassingly, I can sing most of the songs you hear at Pororo Park in Marina Square.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I know that life has changed when I now subconsciously start singing Pororo songs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Life has also changed for me from having tea parties with the Prime Minister and the Ministers to now having weekly tea parties with my daughter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The tea parties are much less stressful now, but those imaginary cups of tea have made it much easier for me to understand my daughter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, life has certainly changed for me now as I am no longer the most stubborn person in my house.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My daughter has learnt to say the word "no" and I never knew that someone could say the word "no" so many times in a day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that she does not change and every guy that approaches her in the future, she will say "no".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As much as I try to live a life without regrets, there will always be regrets, always a wish that we could have done things better, and always a wish that we could have spent more time with our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And as recently published in a The Straits Times article, "Regret is an incurable ache".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The time spent with our children is precious and should be cherished.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The memories created will last forever and are priceless.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot get back the hours, the minutes and the seconds lost.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we can, every day, treasure and value the time we have with our children and our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a journey we must all take together and the only regret one will have is that they did not participate in this journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is everything." Madam, I wholeheartedly support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have all been concerned about our birth rates for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are not the only country that is affected by it.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many of the suggestions come from both sides of the House and many members of the public out there.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And many ideas, many different suggestions; some initiatives are carried out in other countries; some have worked better; some have not worked as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Sometimes, it is also contextual and depending on the cultural context.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Broadly, we do want to look at not just carrots and sticks, but really the overall environment is important.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ultimately, the last and final step must be taken by individuals and their families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What we can do is to provide as supportive an environment as possible.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As whether we are reactive or not, I am also hopeful.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The approach that we have taken really is not about being reactive.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think the reactive part happened quite some time ago and we saw the trends turning into the direction which we were not quite happy with.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Each time, as we see the effect and if it did take effect, we continued to calibrate and improve.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is something that we intend to do.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I do call on all Members in this House who still have some way to go in terms of contributing to the data, well, please.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I would imagine Mr Louis Ng and Ms Tin Pei Ling would help us on that front as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is something that we all have a part to play.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In terms of environment and culture, it is not something that is just mandated by the Government.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is something that is created by all of us as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We know that this has been an issue that many have been championing for some time.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is something I personally felt very strongly about.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I have noted that they would like the Government to extend to unwed mothers the same high level of support we give to married mothers on all fronts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But before I address this point, let me reiterate the key principles underlying our decision for the review on support for unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Lastly, it is also important for us to remember that we do want to encourage families to have children within the confines of parenthood and within the confines of marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think this is to the prevailing prevalent social norm and we all would agree that it is always best for children to grow up in that environment and that is something  we want to continue to encourage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think we have said this several times, but I would like to repeat this here again that it is important to note that while there might be some differentiation for unwed parents, the children of these unwed parents do continue to be provided for on many fronts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It would be not correct to say that they are deprived of everything else.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have equalised some of it in my recent moves.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But I want to emphasise that we do want to support the growth and development of all Singapore Citizen children, regardless of the marital status of their parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And this has been the case for some time.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While we do what we can for the children, we do think that we must continue to try and encourage and support parenthood within the confines of marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many of us would agree that it would always be ideal if children can grow up within the confines of that.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But having said, we do recognise that situations do happen and we want to support the children and we do want to support the families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For vulnerable, low-income unwed parents who need more assistance, my Ministry and the NCSS will work with relevant VWOs and agencies to strengthen support for them and their families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Previously, many of us here, as MPs, we will meet some of our residents who fall under difficult circumstances and unwed mums.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And notwithstanding the fact that there were some differences in some of those various benefits, there is always wholehearted support in terms of providing for them when they do need that help.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members will also remember that we are starting the KidSTART programme that I shared in Parliament last month.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Through this programme, we will proactively identify low-income and vulnerable children aged six and below, and many of these would include children of unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is a very substantive effort and I hope that this is something that would take off because I think it will have a significant impact over the long haul.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng has supported the amendment to allow employers and self-employed persons to claim reimbursement and loss of income, respectively, for the second week of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In fact, he would like employers to actively encourage their employees to take it.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: More importantly, the support you give your staff to better manage their work-life responsibilities will enhance their loyalty and productivity as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Employers who go the extra mile will also attract talent, especially in today's tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On the point of active fatherhood, Mr Louis Ng shared passionately about his experiences, and many of us here who are parents would fully understand his sentiments.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He shared with us what Jill Smokler had to say about this journey.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: My challenge to fellow fathers is to find this out for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There are no shortcuts and we should spend time and effort to be good fathers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I personally believe that it is not just about quality time, but it is also about quantity time.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We must try to be present in our children's lives as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We can do all we can in terms of schemes, in terms of measures to support.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But many of us will also know that we do have choices to make.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Oftentimes, we cite reasons like work and so on.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But sometimes, we are also distracted by our own preoccupations.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The question is: are we prepared to put in the sacrifices?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Are we prepared to put in the time?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Instead of spending time with our friends watching football somewhere else, spending time with children and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And I think as we scroll down and actually study the kind of commitments that we are committed to and we find ourselves busy with, we will find that there are things there that we can actually choose to forgo in favour of time spent with family.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng hit the nail on the head when he shared that the time with our children is precious.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Many of us whose children have grown up or continued to grow up, obviously, we do miss those days when they were toddlers and, each stage, as it moves on, does not ever come back and these will become memories for life, and it is important for us to be there to cherish it when those memories are created.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, it is important for us to be more active and to play a vigilant role.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But we can also take heart that what we have done, when we have done what we can to expose our children to the right values, while there is no guarantee in terms of outcomes but, at least, we have given it our best shot and it is a continuing lifelong journey that we journey with our children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But we all know that the building blocks of any nation really lies with the individuals and the families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If we have strong families, it gives us a reason to be anchored here, it gives us a reason to build a better future.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is not just for ourselves but it is really very much for our families, for our children, and for their children in turn.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will continue as much as we can to create a pro-family environment for families, and to also support the more vulnerable in our society.
